title: Τὸ τόξον τῶν μνηστήρων
titleEn: The Suitors Try the Bow — Odyssey 21.101–206
about: Telemachus takes up Penelope's challenge and asks the suitors to try the bow, saying that if he strings it his mother will not leave. He sets up the axes in a trench, takes his stand at the threshold and three times almost strings the bow, until Odysseus signals him to stop. He gives way and sits down. Antinous orders the trial to go round to the right, and Leiodes, the suitors' priest, is the first to fail; he warns that the bow will kill many of them. Antinous scolds him and sends Melanthius for fire and tallow to soften the bow, but the young men still cannot string it. Antinous and Eurymachus hold back. Meanwhile Odysseus slips out after the cowherd and the swineherd, and asks whom they would defend if he were to come home; both pray for his return, and once he has recognised their loyalty he speaks to them again.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειφ’ ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο·
sentences.l: And to them then spoke the sacred force of Telemachus:
sentences.i: And the strong, sacred figure of Telemachus spoke to them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is a pronoun in the dative plural, ‘to them’: the suitors. μετέειφ’ is μετέειπε ‘spoke among’, with the final vowel dropped before ἱερή and the π turned to φ by the rough breathing that follows. ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο, literally ‘the sacred force of Telemachus’, is a periphrasis: Homer names the hero by the power he has, and the translation keeps both the noun and its epithet every time. Τηλεμάχοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου). The whole line is one the poem has used before; the speech it introduces begins in the next unit.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα με Ζεὺς ἄφρονα θῆκε Κρονίων·
sentences.l: “Ah! Truly me Zeus senseless has made, the son of Cronus;
sentences.i: “Ah, Zeus the son of Cronus has truly made me senseless;
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι, with the circumflex, is a cry of dismay or surprise, ‘Ah’; it is not the ὦ of address. ἦ μάλα is ‘truly, indeed’, and με is ‘me’, the object of θῆκε, the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι (Attic ἔθηκε), which here takes a second accusative, ἄφρονα: ‘made me senseless’. ἄφρων is built from ἀ- ‘without’ and φρήν ‘wits’ and is rendered ‘senseless’ wherever it comes. Κρονίων is a patronymic, ‘son of Cronus’, used as a bare epithet of Ζεύς. The speaker calls himself a fool and goes on to say that he laughs at news that should grieve him.

sentences.t:
μήτηρ μέν μοί φησι φίλη, πινυτή περ ἐοῦσα,
ἄλλῳ ἅμ’ ἕψεσθαι νοσφισσαμένη τόδε δῶμα·
sentences.l:
Mother indeed to me says, dear, though being discerning,
with another to follow, having forsaken this house;
sentences.i: My dear mother, discerning though she is, tells me she will follow another and forsake this house;
sentences.n: μήτηρ is the subject of both φησι ‘she says’ and ἕψεσθαι, so the infinitive carries her own plan: ‘she says that she will follow’. μοι is the dative ‘to me’. φίλη is the stock ‘dear’. πινυτή is ‘discerning’, and περ with the participle ἐοῦσα (Attic οὖσα) gives it concessive force: ‘discerning though she is’. ἕψεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἕπομαι, ‘will follow’, and ἅμ’ ἄλλῳ is ‘along with another’ (ἅμα elided). νοσφισσαμένη is the aorist middle participle of νοσφίζομαι ‘turn away from, forsake’, and takes τόδε δῶμα ‘this house’ as its object. The line does not say who the other man is.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ γελόω καὶ τέρπομαι ἄφρονι θυμῷ.
sentences.l: but I laugh and delight myself with a senseless heart.
sentences.i: but I laugh and enjoy myself, with a senseless heart.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is the epic ‘but’, setting the speaker against his mother. γελόω is an epic form of γελάω (Attic γελῶ), and τέρπομαι is middle, ‘take pleasure’. ἄφρονι θυμῷ is a dative of manner, ‘with a senseless heart’, using the adjective of line 102. Whether the self-mockery is sincere or a pose, the speech turns at once to a proposal.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετε, μνηστῆρες, ἐπεὶ τόδε φαίνετ’ ἄεθλον,
οἵη νῦν οὐκ ἔστι γυνὴ κατ’ Ἀχαιΐδα γαῖαν,
οὔτε Πύλου ἱερῆς οὔτ’ Ἄργεος οὔτε Μυκήνης·
οὔτ’ αὐτῆς Ἰθάκης οὔτ’ ἠπείροιο μελαίνης·
sentences.i: Come then, suitors, since this contest has now appeared—a woman such as now there is none in all the Achaean country, neither of sacred Pylos nor of Argos nor of Mycenae, nor of Ithaca itself nor of the dark mainland;
sentences.n: The opening line is the one Penelope used at 21.73 to launch the contest; Telemachus takes up her words. ἀλλ’ ἄγετε is the plural of ‘come now’, a call to act. φαίνετ’ is φαίνεται, ‘has appeared’. ἄεθλον (Attic ἆθλον) is ‘contest’, here the bow-trial and its prize together. οἵη is a feminine relative, ‘such as’, and looks to γυνή: the construction is loose, and the prize the contest offers is a woman unmatched anywhere. Ἀχαιΐδα is a feminine adjective ‘Achaean’, and γαῖα is rendered ‘country’. Πύλου ἱερῆς is ‘sacred Pylos’, ἱερῆς being a feminine genitive. The places run from the Peloponnese to Ithaca itself and the ἤπειρος ‘mainland’ across the water, where μέλαινα ‘dark’ is used of the earth. οὔτε … οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor … nor’.

sentences.t: καὶ δ’ αὐτοὶ τόδε γ’ ἴστε· τί με χρὴ μητέρος αἴνου;
sentences.l: And indeed you yourselves know this at least; why have I need of my mother’s praise?
sentences.i: You yourselves know this well enough; what need have I to praise my mother?
sentences.n: καὶ δ’ is ‘and indeed’, αὐτοί is ‘you yourselves’, and τόδε γ’ is ‘this at least’; ἴστε is the second plural of οἶδα. χρή here takes an accusative of the person (με) and a genitive of what is needed (αἴνου), ‘what need is there for me of …’. αἶνος is ‘praise’ here, though the word also means ‘tale’. The sense is that the suitors know her worth already, so he need not describe it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μὴ μύνῃσι παρέλκετε μηδ’ ἔτι τόξου
δηρὸν ἀποτρωπᾶσθε τανυστύος, ὄφρα ἴδωμεν.
sentences.l:
But come, do not with excuses keep dragging it out, nor any more of the bow
for long turn away from the stringing, so that we may see.
sentences.i: But come now, do not keep dragging matters out with excuses, nor go on turning away from the stringing of the bow any longer, so that we may see.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come now’, with ἄγε in its frozen singular form, though the suitors are many; at 106 the plural ἄγετε was used. μὴ … παρέλκετε is a prohibition with the present imperative, ‘do not keep …’; παρέλκω is ‘drag aside, protract’ (ἕλκω ‘drag’ with παρά), here with no object. μύνῃσι is the dative plural of μύνη, a rare word usually glossed ‘pretext, excuse’; its derivation is not known. ἀποτρωπᾶσθε is a contracted imperative of ἀποτρωπάω, a frequentative of ἀποτρέπω, ‘keep turning away from’, and takes the genitive τανυστύος, a rare noun ‘stringing’ from τανύω, which in turn takes τόξου: ‘the stringing of the bow’. ὄφρα ἴδωμεν is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive.

sentences.t: καὶ δέ κεν αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τοῦ τόξου πειρησαίμην·
sentences.l: and indeed I myself might make trial of the bow;
sentences.i: I myself, too, might try the bow;
sentences.n: καὶ δέ is ‘and indeed’, αὐτὸς ἐγώ ‘I myself’. κεν marks the optative πειρησαίμην, the aorist middle of πειράω, as an intention or possibility: ‘I might try’. It takes the genitive τοῦ τόξου, and τοῦ is still a demonstrative, ‘that bow there’, not a bare article.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν ἐντανύσω διοϊστεύσω τε σιδήρου,
οὔ κέ μοι ἀχνυμένῳ τάδε δώματα πότνια μήτηρ
λείποι ἅμ’ ἄλλῳ ἰοῦσ’, ὅτ’ ἐγὼ κατόπισθε λιποίμην
οἷός τ’ ἤδη πατρὸς ἀέθλια κάλ’ ἀνελέσθαι.
sentences.l:
but if I string it and shoot through the iron,
not to me grieving would this house my lady mother
leave, going along with another, when I should be left behind
already such as to take up my father’s fine contest-prizes.”
sentences.i: But if I string it and shoot through the iron, my lady mother would not, to my grief, leave this house and go off with another, when I should be left behind, already able to carry off my father’s fine prizes from contests.”
sentences.n: εἰ … κεν with the subjunctives ἐντανύσω and διοϊστεύσω is ‘if ever I string it and shoot through’ (Attic ἐάν); the conclusion is οὔ κε λείποι, an optative with κε, ‘she would not leave’. διοϊστεύσω takes σιδήρου, the iron of the axes, as in the previous part. ἀχνυμένῳ ‘grieving’ agrees with μοι. δώματα is a poetic plural for the one dwelling, rendered ‘house’; πότνια μήτηρ is ‘my lady mother’. ἰοῦσ’ is the participle of εἶμι, ‘going’. ὅτ’ ἐγὼ κατόπισθε λιποίμην is another optative, ‘when I should be left behind’, and οἷός τ’ is ‘such as to, able to’, with ἀνελέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of ἀναιρέω, ‘take up, carry off’. ἀέθλια are contest-prizes; whether the phrase means the bow-trial itself or his father’s winnings is not certain. This ends the first part of the speech.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ ἀπ’ ὤμοιϊν χλαῖναν θέτο φοινικόεσσαν
ὀρθὸς ἀναΐξας, ἀπὸ δὲ ξίφος ὀξὺ θέτ’ ὤμων.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and from his shoulders put off the crimson cloak,
springing upright, and from his shoulders put off the sharp sword.
sentences.i: So he said, and springing upright he put the crimson cloak off his shoulders, and the sharp sword too.
sentences.n: ἦ καί is ‘he spoke, and’ (ἦ from ἠμί ‘say’), the formula that closes a speech. ἀπ’ … θέτο is tmesis: ἀπό stands apart from θέτο, the unaugmented aorist middle of τίθημι, and together they mean ‘put off’; the same verb returns in the second half of the line with ἀπὸ … θέτ’. ὤμοιϊν is an epic form of ‘shoulders’ with an old ending in -οιϊν (Attic ὤμων or ὤμοις). ὀρθὸς ἀναΐξας is ‘having sprung upright’. φοινικόεσσαν is ‘crimson’, and ξίφος ὀξύ is ‘the sharp sword’. He strips to move freely.

sentences.t:
πρῶτον μὲν πελέκεας στῆσεν, διὰ τάφρον ὀρύξας
πᾶσι μίαν μακρήν, καὶ ἐπὶ στάθμην ἴθυνεν,
ἀμφὶ δὲ γαῖαν ἔναξε·
sentences.i: First he set up the axes, having dug one long trench for them all, and made them straight to the line, and packed the earth down around them;
sentences.n: πελέκεας is the accusative plural of πέλεκυς ‘axe’ (Attic πελέκεις); these are the axes of the contest. διὰ … ὀρύξας is tmesis for διορύξας, ‘having dug through’, with τάφρον ‘trench’ as its object; πᾶσι μίαν μακρήν is ‘one long one for all of them’, a single trench for the whole row. στάθμη is a builder’s line, and ἐπὶ στάθμην ἴθυνεν is ‘made them straight to the line’ (ἰθύνω). ἀμφί is an adverb, ‘around’, and ἔναξε is an aorist of νάσσω ‘pack down, stamp firm’: he tamped the earth round them.

sentences.t:
τάφος δ’ ἕλε πάντας ἰδόντας,
ὡς εὐκόσμως στῆσε·
sentences.l:
and amazement took all, having seen
how in good order he set them up;
sentences.i: and amazement seized all who saw how in good order he set them up;
sentences.n: τάφος here is ‘amazement’, a different word from the better-known τάφος ‘grave’. ἕλε is the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω, ‘seized’ (Attic εἷλε), and ἰδόντας, the aorist participle, agrees with πάντας: ‘all who saw’. ὡς is ‘how’, introducing what they saw; εὐκόσμως is ‘in good order’; στῆσε is the same verb as στῆσεν two lines before, ‘set up’.

sentences.t: πάρος δ’ οὐ πώ ποτ’ ὀπώπει.
sentences.l: for before not yet ever had he seen it.
sentences.i: for he had never seen it done before.
sentences.n: πάρος is the adverb ‘before’, and οὐ πώ ποτε is ‘never yet’. ὀπώπει is the pluperfect of the old perfect ὄπωπα of ὁράω, with the force of a simple past, ‘had seen’. The Greek leaves both its subject and its object unstated; I take the subject to be Telemachus, who had never seen such a thing done, but the line could also be read as ‘no one had ever seen’ it.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰὼν καὶ τόξου πειρήτιζε.
sentences.l: And he stood on the threshold, going, and of the bow was making trial.
sentences.i: And he went and stood on the threshold and tried the bow.
sentences.n: στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι, ‘stood’ (Attic ἔστη); δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and then’. ἰών is the participle of εἶμι, ‘going’, and the οὐδός is the threshold. πειρήτιζε is the imperfect of πειρητίζω ‘try, make trial of’, with the genitive τόξου; the imperfect, ‘was trying’, prepares the three attempts that follow. The English layer says ‘tried’.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μέν μιν πελέμιξεν ἐρύσσεσθαι μενεαίνων,
τρὶς δὲ μεθῆκε βίης, ἐπιελπόμενος τό γε θυμῷ,
νευρὴν ἐντανύειν διοϊστεύσειν τε σιδήρου.
sentences.l:
Three times indeed he made it shake, eager to draw it,
three times and he let go of his force, hoping this in his heart,
to string the bowstring and to shoot through the iron.
sentences.i: Three times he made it quiver, straining to draw it, and three times he slackened his strength, hoping in his heart that he would string the bowstring and shoot an arrow through the iron.
sentences.n: τρίς is ‘three times’, and μιν is ‘it’, the bow. πελέμιξεν is the aorist of πελεμίζω ‘make shake’. ἐρύσσεσθαι is the middle infinitive of ἐρύω ‘draw, pull’, and μενεαίνων ‘straining, eager’ is from μενεαίνω, built on μένος. μεθῆκε βίης is ‘let go of force’: μεθίημι takes a genitive, ‘slackened his effort’. ἐπιελπόμενος τό γε θυμῷ is ‘hoping this in his heart’, with τό standing for the clause that follows. ἐντανύειν is a present infinitive and διοϊστεύσειν a future one; the pair does not match in tense, but the sense is plain, and the two verbs repeat those of 21.96–97.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κε δή ῥ’ ἐτάνυσσε βίῃ τὸ τέταρτον ἀνέλκων,
ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ἀνένευε καὶ ἔσχεθεν ἱέμενόν περ.
sentences.l:
And now indeed he would have strung it by force, the fourth time pulling up,
but Odysseus signed a refusal and held him back, eager though he was.
sentences.i: And now he would indeed have strung it by force on the fourth pull, but Odysseus made a sign of refusal and held him back, eager though he was.
sentences.n: καί νύ κε δή ῥα with the imperfect ἐτάνυσσε is ‘and now he would have strung it’: an imperfect with κε describes something that very nearly happened. ἐτάνυσσε has a doubled σ for the metre (= ἐτάνυσε). τὸ τέταρτον is ‘the fourth time’, and ἀνέλκων ‘pulling up’. ἀνένευε is the imperfect of ἀνανεύω ‘throw the head back’, the gesture of refusal, so ‘made a sign of refusal’. ἔσχεθεν is an extended epic aorist of ἔχω, ‘held back’. ἱέμενόν περ is ‘eager though’, accusative because it agrees with the unexpressed ‘him’. The signal comes from Odysseus alone; the text gives no reason.

sentences.t: τοῖς δ’ αὖτις μετέειφ’ ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο·
sentences.l: Then among them again spoke the sacred force of Telemachus:
sentences.i: The strong, sacred figure of Telemachus spoke among them again:
sentences.n: τοῖς is the pronoun ‘to them’, the suitors, and αὖτις ‘again’. μετέειφ’ is μετέειπε, as at 101, and the periphrasis ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο is translated as before. The line differs from 101 only in τοῖς δ’ αὖτις for τοῖσι δὲ καί, and it brings Telemachus back to speak a second time after being stopped.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ καὶ ἔπειτα κακός τ’ ἔσομαι καὶ ἄκικυς,
ἠὲ νεώτερός εἰμι καὶ οὔ πω χερσὶ πέποιθα
ἄνδρ’ ἀπαμύνασθαι, ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ.
sentences.l:
“Ah! Truly even hereafter both base shall I be and feeble,
or younger am I, and not yet in my hands do I trust
to ward off a man, when anyone first grows angry.
sentences.i: “Ah, am I to be base and feeble even hereafter, or am I too young, and do I not yet trust my hands to ward off a man, whenever someone is the first to grow angry?
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is the cry of 102. I take ἦ … ἠέ as the two members of a double question, ‘is it that … or that …’, though the edition ends the unit with a full stop. ἦ καὶ ἔπειτα is ‘even hereafter’, with the future ἔσομαι. κακός is ‘base, of no worth’, and ἄκικυς is a rare word usually glossed ‘feeble’; its derivation is not known. νεώτερος is the comparative ‘younger, too young’. πέποιθα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I trust’, with the dative χερσί. ἀπαμύνασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive ‘to ward off’, with ἄνδρ’ as object; ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ is ‘whenever anyone first grows angry’. These last words repeat an earlier speech of Telemachus.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’, οἵ περ ἐμεῖο βίῃ προφερέστεροί ἐστε,
τόξου πειρήσασθε, καὶ ἐκτελέωμεν ἄεθλον.
sentences.l:
But come, you who than me in force are stronger,
of the bow make trial, and let us bring to an end the contest.”
sentences.i: But come, you who are stronger than I am, try the bow, and let us bring the contest to its end.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ is ‘but come’, the plural of ἄγε. οἵ περ … ἐστε is a relative clause, ‘you who are’. ἐμεῖο is a genitive of comparison (Attic ἐμοῦ), ‘than I’, with προφερέστεροι, the comparative of πρόφερος ‘better, superior’, and the dative βίῃ ‘in force’. πειρήσασθε is the aorist middle imperative ‘try’. ἐκτελέωμεν is an aorist subjunctive of exhortation, ‘let us bring to an end’; the uncontracted -έω- is the epic form (Attic ἐκτελῶμεν). With this he gives up the bow to the suitors.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν τόξον μὲν ἀπὸ ἕο θῆκε χαμᾶζε,
κλίνας κολλητῇσιν ἐϋξέστῃς σανίδεσσιν,
αὐτοῦ δ’ ὠκὺ βέλος καλῇ προσέκλινε κορώνῃ,
ἂψ δ’ αὖτις κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετ’ ἐπὶ θρόνου ἔνθεν ἀνέστη.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, the bow indeed from himself he set down to the ground,
leaning it on well-joined, well-polished boards,
and there the swift arrow to the fair handle he leaned,
and back again he sat down upon the chair from which he had risen.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and set the bow down on the ground away from himself, leaning it against the well-joined, well-polished boards, and right there leaned the swift arrow against the fair handle, and went back and sat down again on the chair he had risen from.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’. ἕο is the reflexive genitive ‘from himself’ (ἀπὸ ἕο), and χαμᾶζε has the suffix -ζε, ‘to the ground’. θῆκε is unaugmented. κλίνας is the aorist participle ‘leaning’. κολλητῇσιν ἐϋξέστῃς σανίδεσσιν are datives in -ῃσιν and -εσσιν: κολλητός is ‘glued, fitted together’, ἐΰξεστος ‘well-polished’, and σανίς a plank. The boards are probably the leaves of the door, since the handle follows, but the text does not say so. κορώνη also means ‘crow’; of a door it is the handle. αὐτοῦ here is the adverb ‘right there’, spelled like the genitive. προσέκλινε is ‘leaned against’. In the last line κατ’ is the preverb of ἕζετο, in tmesis, ‘sat down’; ἂψ δ’ αὖτις is ‘back again’, and ἔνθεν ‘from where’.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀντίνοος μετέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός·
sentences.l: Among them then spoke Antinous, Eupeithes’ son:
sentences.i: Among them Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke:
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is the dative plural of the pronoun, ‘among them’. μετέφη is the aorist of μετα-φημί, ‘spoke among’. Εὐπείθεος is a genitive in -εος (Attic -ους), so Εὐπείθεος υἱός is ‘son of Eupeithes’: the patronymic is the fixed way of naming Antinous when he speaks.

sentences.t:
ὄρνυσθ’ ἑξείης ἐπιδέξια πάντες ἑταῖροι,
ἀρξάμενοι τοῦ χώρου ὅθεν τέ περ οἰνοχοεύει.
sentences.l:
“Rouse yourselves one after another, to the right, all companions,
beginning from the place whence he pours the wine.”
sentences.i: “Rise, all you companions, one after another and to the right, beginning from the place where the wine is poured.”
sentences.n: ὄρνυσθ’ is the middle imperative of ὄρνυμι, ‘rouse yourselves’. ἑξείης is ‘in order, one after another’, and ἐπιδέξια ‘to the right’; the order of trying the bow follows the order in which the wine goes round. ἑταῖροι is a vocative, ‘companions’. ἀρξάμενοι is the aorist middle participle ‘beginning’. τοῦ χώρου ὅθεν τέ περ is ‘from the very place from which’, and οἰνοχοεύει ‘pours wine’ has no stated subject: the cupbearer.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀντίνοος, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπιήνδανε μῦθος.
sentences.l: So spoke Antinous, and to them the word was pleasing.
sentences.i: So spoke Antinous, and his words pleased them.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφατο elided), the formula that closes a speech and names the speaker. τοῖσιν is a pronoun, ‘to them’. ἐπιήνδανε is the imperfect of ἐπιανδάνω ‘be pleasing to’, with the dative, and μῦθος is ‘word, speech, proposal’.

sentences.t:
Λειώδης δὲ πρῶτος ἀνίστατο, Οἴνοπος υἱός,
ὅ σφι θυοσκόος ἔσκε, παρὰ κρητῆρα δὲ καλὸν
ἷζε μυχοίτατος αἰέν·
sentences.i: Leiodes, son of Oenops, was the first to rise; he was their sacrificing priest, and he always sat in the innermost place by the fair mixing-bowl;
sentences.n: Λειώδης is Leiodes. Οἴνοπος is the genitive of Οἴνωψ, so Οἴνοπος υἱός is ‘son of Oenops’. πρῶτος is a predicate, ‘was the first to’, with the imperfect middle ἀνίστατο ‘rose up’. ὅ is here the old article-form used as a relative, ‘who’; σφι is the dative ‘for them’. θυοσκόος is a priest who attends the offerings; the exact function is not certain. ἔσκε is an iterative form of εἰμί, ‘used to be’. ἷζε is ‘sat’; μυχοίτατος is the superlative of μύχιος ‘innermost’, and αἰέν is αἰεί ‘always’. κρητῆρα is the mixing-bowl, and καλόν agrees with it.

sentences.t:
ἀτασθαλίαι δέ οἱ οἴῳ
ἐχθραὶ ἔσαν, πᾶσιν δὲ νεμέσσα μνηστήρεσσιν·
sentences.l:
and wanton-follies to him alone
hateful were, and at all the suitors he felt resentment;
sentences.i: wanton folly was hateful to him alone, and he felt resentment at all the suitors;
sentences.n: ἀτασθαλίαι is the plural of the noun of 1.7, ‘wanton-follies’. οἱ is the enclitic dative ‘to him’, and οἴῳ ‘alone’ agrees with it. ἐχθραί is ‘hateful’, and ἔσαν is ἦσαν. νεμέσσα is the imperfect of νεμεσσάω ‘feel resentment at’ (the σ is doubled for the metre), and it takes the dative πᾶσιν … μνηστήρεσσιν. The unit begins in the middle of line 146, after the ano teleia that closes the previous sentence.

sentences.t: ὅς ῥα τότε πρῶτος τόξον λάβε καὶ βέλος ὠκύ.
sentences.l: who then first took the bow and the swift arrow.
sentences.i: It was he who then first took the bow and the swift arrow.
sentences.n: ὅς here is the relative, resuming the sentence and giving the sense ‘it was he who’; ῥα is the particle that marks a thing as expected. λάβε is the unaugmented aorist of λαμβάνω (Attic ἔλαβε). ὠκὺ βέλος is ‘swift arrow’, and βέλος is any missile; the same words come again at 138.

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰὼν καὶ τόξου πειρήτιζεν,
οὐδέ μιν ἐντάνυσε·
sentences.l:
And he stood on the threshold, going, and of the bow was making trial,
and did not string it;
sentences.i: And he went and stood on the threshold and tried the bow, and did not string it;
sentences.n: The first half repeats line 124 except for the nu at the end of πειρήτιζεν. μιν is ‘it’, the bow, the object of ἐντάνυσε, the aorist of ἐντανύω ‘string’. οὐδέ … ἐντάνυσε is a plain statement of failure, and the next unit says why.

sentences.t:
πρὶν γὰρ κάμε χεῖρας ἀνέλκων
ἀτρίπτους ἁπαλάς·
sentences.l:
for sooner he wearied his hands, drawing up,
unrubbed ones, soft ones;
sentences.i: for his hands, unworn and soft, grew weary first as he pulled it up;
sentences.n: πρίν here is an adverb, ‘sooner, first’: his hands gave out before the bow yielded. κάμε is the unaugmented aorist of κάμνω ‘grow tired’, with χεῖρας as an accusative of respect: ‘he tired in the hands’. ἀνέλκων is ‘drawing up’. ἀτρίπτους ‘unrubbed, unworn’ is from τρίβω ‘rub’, and ἁπαλάς is ‘soft’; both agree with χεῖρας. The picture is of a priest’s hands, never worn by work.

sentences.t: μετὰ δὲ μνηστῆρσιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: and among the suitors he said:
sentences.i: and he spoke among the suitors:
sentences.n: μετά with the dative μνηστῆρσιν is ‘among the suitors’ (the short dative plural -ρσιν). ἔειπεν is an epic aorist of εἶπον, ‘said’, with the vowel doubled. The speech follows.

sentences.t: ὦ φίλοι, οὐ μὲν ἐγὼ τανύω, λαβέτω δὲ καὶ ἄλλος.
sentences.l: “O friends, I indeed am not stringing it; but let another take it too.
sentences.i: “Friends, I am not stringing it; let someone else take it up.
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is ‘friends’; ὦ is the particle of address. οὐ μὲν ἐγώ is ‘I, for one, do not’. τανύω is a present, ‘I am stringing’, and means that he gives up the attempt. λαβέτω is the aorist imperative ‘let him take’, and καὶ ἄλλος ‘another as well’.

sentences.t:
πολλοὺς γὰρ τόδε τόξον ἀριστῆας κεκαδήσει
θυμοῦ καὶ ψυχῆς, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτερόν ἐστι
τεθνάμεν ἢ ζώοντας ἁμαρτεῖν, οὗθ’ ἕνεκ’ αἰεὶ
ἐνθάδ’ ὁμιλέομεν, ποτιδέγμενοι ἤματα πάντα.
sentences.l:
For many best men this bow will deprive
of heart and of life, since truly it is far better
to be dead than, living, to miss that for the sake of which always
here we assemble, waiting all our days.
sentences.i: For this bow will deprive many of our best men of heart and life, since it is truly far better to be dead than to live and miss the thing for whose sake we are always gathered here, waiting all our days.
sentences.n: ἀριστῆας is ‘best men’. κεκαδήσει is a future formed on the reduplicated aorist stem of χάζω ‘yield’; it is a rare causative ‘make give up, deprive’, and takes the genitive θυμοῦ καὶ ψυχῆς, ‘of heart and of life’; ψυχή is ‘life’ here. ἐπεὶ ἦ is ‘since truly’, and φέρτερον is ‘better’. τεθνάμεν is the perfect infinitive ‘to be dead’ (Attic τεθνάναι), ζώοντας the participle ‘while living’, and ἁμαρτεῖν the aorist infinitive ‘to miss, fail of’, with the genitive οὗ in οὗθ’ ἕνεκ’ = οὗ ἕνεκα ‘for whose sake’. The thing is not named until 157–158. ὁμιλέομεν is uncontracted (Attic ὁμιλοῦμεν), and ποτιδέγμενοι ‘waiting’ is a participle of προσδέχομαι with the epic ποτί; ἤματα πάντα is ‘all our days’.

sentences.t:
νῦν μέν τις καὶ ἔλπετ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ἠδὲ μενοινᾷ
γῆμαι Πηνελόπειαν, Ὀδυσσῆος παράκοιτιν.
sentences.l:
Now indeed someone both hopes in his wits and longs
to marry Penelope, the consort of Odysseus.
sentences.i: At present one man or another hopes in his mind and longs to marry Penelope, the wife of Odysseus.
sentences.n: νῦν μέν is ‘now indeed’, answered by αὐτάρ at the start of the next unit. τις is ‘someone’, here ‘one man or another’. ἔλπετ’ is ἔλπεται, ‘hopes’, with ἐνὶ φρεσίν ‘in his mind’, and μενοινᾷ is the contracted third singular of μενοινάω ‘long for’; both take the infinitive γῆμαι, the aorist of γαμέω ‘to marry’, said of a man. Πηνελόπειαν is the Homeric spelling of Penelope’s name. παράκοιτις is ‘bedfellow, consort’, and Ὀδυσσῆος is a genitive.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν τόξου πειρήσεται ἠδὲ ἴδηται,
ἄλλην δή τιν’ ἔπειτα Ἀχαιϊάδων εὐπέπλων
μνάσθω ἐέδνοισιν διζήμενος·
sentences.i: but when he has tried the bow and seen it, let him then court some other of the fair-robed Achaean women, seeking her with bridal gifts;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπήν is ‘but when’, the Attic ἐπάν. πειρήσεται is a future and ἴδηται an aorist subjunctive; the two stand side by side after ἐπήν. ἄλλην δή τιν’ is ‘some other, then’, and Ἀχαιϊάδων εὐπέπλων is a partitive genitive plural, ‘of the fair-robed Achaean women’; εὐπέπλων is from πέπλος ‘robe’. μνάσθω is the third singular imperative of μνάομαι ‘woo’, contracted from μνάεσθω. ἐέδνοισιν is a dative plural of ἔεδνα ‘bridal gifts’, ‘with gifts’, and διζήμενος is ‘seeking’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δέ κ’ ἔπειτα
γήμαιθ’ ὅς κε πλεῖστα πόροι καὶ μόρσιμος ἔλθοι.
sentences.l:
and she then might marry
whoever should give the most and come as the destined one.”
sentences.i: and she may then marry whichever man gives most and comes as the destined one.”
sentences.n: ἡ δέ is ‘and she’, the other woman, again a pronoun. γήμαιθ’ is γήμαιτο, the aorist middle optative of γαμέω, said of a woman marrying; with κε it means ‘might marry’. ὅς κε πλεῖστα πόροι is ‘whoever might give the most’, a relative with the optative, and πλεῖστα ‘the most’. μόρσιμος is ‘destined, fated’, built on μόρος ‘lot’; with ἔλθοι it is ‘comes as the destined one’. This ends Leiodes’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν καὶ ἀπὸ ἕο τόξον ἔθηκε,
κλίνας κολλητῇσιν ἐϋξέστῃς σανίδεσσιν,
αὐτοῦ δ’ ὠκὺ βέλος καλῇ προσέκλινε κορώνῃ,
ἂψ δ’ αὖτις κατ’ ἄρ ἕζετ’ ἐπὶ θρόνου ἔνθεν ἀνέστη.
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and from himself the bow he set down,
leaning it on well-joined, well-polished boards,
and there the swift arrow to the fair handle he leaned,
and back again he sat down upon the chair from which he had risen.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and set the bow down away from himself, leaning it against the well-joined, well-polished boards, and right there leaned the swift arrow against the fair handle, and went back and sat down again on the chair he had risen from.
sentences.n: Leiodes does exactly what Telemachus did at 136–139, and the lines repeat almost word for word. ἐφώνησεν is ‘spoke aloud’, and ἔθηκε is the augmented form of the aorist of τίθημι, where 136 had the unaugmented θῆκε. The edition prints κατ’ ἄρ in the last line without the elision mark it uses at 139; the words are the same.

sentences.t: Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἐνένιπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.l: And Antinous rebuked them, and spoke a word and called them by name:
sentences.i: And Antinous rebuked them, and spoke, calling them by name:
sentences.n: The line is a formula already shipped. ἐνένιπεν is the imperfect of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’, and the Greek states no object. The English ‘them’ is the shipped wording of the formula, fixed from a line where the rebuke fell on two men; here the one rebuked is Leiodes, whom Antinous names in the next line. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is the formula ‘spoke a word and called by name’, with ἔκ in tmesis.

sentences.t:
Λειῶδες, ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων,
δεινόν τ’ ἀργαλέον τε, —νεμεσσῶμαι δέ τ’ ἀκούων—
εἰ δὴ τοῦτό γε τόξον ἀριστῆας κεκαδήσει
θυμοῦ καὶ ψυχῆς, ἐπεὶ οὐ δύνασαι σὺ τανύσσαι.
sentences.l:
“Leiodes, what sort of word has escaped you past the fence of your teeth,
dreadful and grievous—and I am resentful at hearing it—
if indeed this bow will deprive the best men
of heart and of life, since you yourself cannot string it.
sentences.i: “Leiodes, what sort of word has escaped you past the fence of your teeth, dreadful and grievous—I am resentful at hearing it—if indeed this bow will deprive the best men of heart and life, because you yourself cannot string it.
sentences.n: Λειῶδες is the vocative of Λειώδης. ποῖον … ἔπος is ‘what sort of word’, an exclamation, though the edition prints no mark. σε is the accusative of the person it has escaped, and ἕρκος ὀδόντων, ‘the fence of the teeth’, is a second accusative saying what it passed. φύγεν is the unaugmented aorist of φεύγω. δεινόν τ’ ἀργαλέον τε is ‘dreadful and grievous’, in apposition to ἔπος. Between the dashes, νεμεσσῶμαι is the middle of νεμεσσάω ‘feel resentment’, and ἀκούων ‘hearing’. εἰ δή follows that verb of feeling and gives the content of the word: ‘if indeed this bow will deprive …’, which repeats lines 153–154. τανύσσαι is the aorist infinitive with doubled σ.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τοί σέ γε τοῖον ἐγείνατο πότνια μήτηρ
οἷόν τε ῥυτῆρα βιοῦ τ’ ἔμεναι καὶ ὀϊστῶν·
sentences.l:
For not indeed you such did bear your lady mother
as to be a drawer of the bow and of arrows;
sentences.i: For your lady mother did not bear you to be the sort of man who draws the bow and its arrows;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ τοί σέ γε is ‘for surely not you’; τοι is a particle here. τοῖον … οἷόν τε is ‘of such a kind … as to’. ἐγείνατο is the aorist middle of γείνομαι, the verb for a mother bearing a child, and πότνια μήτηρ is ‘lady mother’. ῥυτῆρα, from ἐρύω ‘draw’, is ‘a drawer’; βιοῦ, accented as ‘bow’ (βίος with the accent on the first syllable is ‘life’), and ὀϊστῶν ‘arrows’ are its genitives. The word ῥυτήρ is rare; the sense is ‘archer’. ἔμεναι is the infinitive ‘to be’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄλλοι τανύουσι τάχα μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί.
sentences.l: but others will string it soon, the noble suitors.”
sentences.i: but others, the noble suitors, will soon string it.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ is ‘no, but’. τανύουσι is a present form, but with τάχα ‘soon’ it has future sense. μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί is the fixed ‘the noble suitors’. The speech ends by turning from Leiodes to the rest of the company.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, καί ῥ’ ἐκέλευσε Μελάνθιον, αἰπόλον αἰγῶν·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and then he ordered Melanthius, the goatherd of goats:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and gave his orders to Melanthius, the goatherd of the goats:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’. καί ῥ’ is ‘and then’. ἐκέλευσε is ‘ordered’, with the accusative Μελάνθιον. αἰπόλον αἰγῶν, ‘goatherd of goats’, repeats itself on purpose: αἰπόλος already contains the word for goat, and the pleonasm is Homer’s fixed way of naming the man.

sentences.t:
ἄγρει δή, πῦρ κῆον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι, Μελανθεῦ,
πὰρ δὲ τίθει δίφρον τε μέγαν καὶ κῶας ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ,
ἐκ δὲ στέατος ἔνεικε μέγαν τροχὸν ἔνδον ἐόντος,
sentences.l:
“Come now, kindle a fire in the halls, Melanthius,
and beside it set a great stool and a fleece upon it,
and out of the tallow bring a great wheel, that is within,
sentences.i: “Come now, kindle a fire in the halls, Melanthius, and set beside it a great stool with a fleece on it, and bring out a great round of the tallow that is within,
sentences.n: ἄγρει is an imperative like ἄγε, ‘come’, and δή ‘now’. κῆον is an imperative of κήω, the epic form of καίω ‘kindle’. ἐνὶ μεγάροισι is ‘in the halls’, a plural for one hall, and Μελανθεῦ is a vocative. In πὰρ δὲ τίθει the preverb stands apart from the verb (tmesis), ‘set beside’. δίφρον is ‘stool’, and κῶας ‘fleece’. ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ is ‘on it’, αὐτοῦ being the pronoun’s genitive. ἐκ … ἔνεικε is tmesis again, and ἔνεικε is the aorist imperative of φέρω, ‘bring out’. στέατος is ‘from the tallow’, a partitive genitive of στέαρ, and τροχόν is literally ‘wheel’, here a large round piece. ἔνδον ἐόντος is ‘being inside’ (ἐόντος = ὄντος).

sentences.t:
ὄφρα νέοι θάλποντες, ἐπιχρίοντες ἀλοιφῇ,
τόξου πειρώμεσθα καὶ ἐκτελέωμεν ἄεθλον.
sentences.l:
so that we young men, warming it, smearing it with fat,
may make trial of the bow and bring to an end the contest.”
sentences.i: so that we young men, warming it and rubbing it with fat, may try the bow and bring the contest to its end.”
sentences.n: ὄφρα is ‘so that’ with the subjunctives πειρώμεσθα and ἐκτελέωμεν. νέοι is ‘we young men’. θάλποντες and ἐπιχρίοντες are present participles, ‘warming’ and ‘smearing over’, and the bow is their unstated object; ἀλοιφῇ is the dative ‘with fat’. The fire, the stool with its fleece and the tallow are for softening the bow. ἐκτελέωμεν is the same verb as at 135.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὁ δ’ αἶψ’ ἀνέκαιε Μελάνθιος ἀκάματον πῦρ,
πὰρ δὲ φέρων δίφρον θῆκεν καὶ κῶας ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ,
ἐκ δὲ στέατος ἔνεικε μέγαν τροχὸν ἔνδον ἐόντος·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Melanthius quickly kindled an untiring fire, and brought a stool and set it beside it, and a fleece upon it, and brought out a great round of the tallow that was within;
sentences.n: ὣς φάθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (φάτο with its vowel elided). ὁ δ’ is ‘and he’, and αἶψ’ ‘quickly’. ἀνέκαιε is ‘kindled up’, and ἀκάματον ‘untiring’ is the fire’s epithet (ἀ- and κάμνω): it is rendered every time. Melanthius does as he is told, almost in the words of the order. ἔνεικε here is an indicative, ‘he brought’ (the aorist ἤνεικε without its augment), where at 178 the same spelling is an imperative.

sentences.t: τῷ ῥα νέοι θάλποντες ἐπειρῶντ’·
sentences.l: Thereupon the young men, warming it, were trying it;
sentences.i: Then the young men warmed the bow and tried it;
sentences.n: τῷ ῥα is ‘thereupon, so’, a dative pronoun used like a conjunction; it might also mean ‘at it’, the fire. The Greek states no object for θάλποντες ‘warming’ or for ἐπειρῶντ(ο), the imperfect middle of πειράω ‘try’; both refer to the bow. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἐδύναντο
ἐντανύσαι, πολλὸν δὲ βίης ἐπιδευέες ἦσαν.
sentences.l:
and they were not able
to string it, and by much of force they were lacking.
sentences.i: but they could not string it, for they fell far short in strength.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἐδύναντο is the imperfect of δύναμαι, ‘they were not able’, with the aorist infinitive ἐντανύσαι ‘to string’. πολλόν is an adverb ‘by much’. ἐπιδευέες is the plural of ἐπιδευής ‘lacking, in want of’, and takes the genitive βίης: ‘lacking in strength’.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἔτ’ ἐπεῖχε καὶ Εὐρύμαχος θεοειδής,
ἀρχοὶ μνηστήρων·
sentences.l:
But Antinous still held back, and Eurymachus, godlike-in-form,
the leaders of the suitors;
sentences.i: Antinous still held back, and so did Eurymachus, godlike in form, the leaders of the suitors;
sentences.n: ἐπεῖχε is the imperfect of ἐπέχω, here intransitive, ‘hold back, hold off’: the two chief suitors have not yet tried. The verb is singular, agreeing with the first-named subject. ἔτ’ is ‘still’. Εὐρύμαχος θεοειδής is fixed: θεοειδής is ‘godlike in form’. ἀρχοί is a nominative plural in apposition to the two names.

sentences.t: ἀρετῇ δ’ ἔσαν ἔξοχ’ ἄριστοι.
sentences.l: and in excellence they were far the best.
sentences.i: and they were far the best of them in excellence.
sentences.n: ἀρετῇ is a dative of respect, ‘in excellence’. ἔσαν is ἦσαν. ἔξοχ’ is ἔξοχα, an adverb ‘beyond others, far’, and ἄριστοι is ‘best’. The words are close to those used of the same two men elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἐξ οἴκου βῆσαν ὁμαρτήσαντες ἅμ’ ἄμφω
βουκόλος ἠδὲ συφορβὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο·
sentences.l:
And those two out of the house went, going together, both,
the cowherd and the swineherd of divine Odysseus;
sentences.i: And the two of them went out of the house together, the cowherd and the swineherd of divine Odysseus;
sentences.n: τώ is the dual of the pronoun, ‘those two’, which βουκόλος and συφορβός then name. βῆσαν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω (Attic ἔβησαν), ‘went’. ὁμαρτήσαντες is the aorist participle of ὁμαρτέω ‘go together’, strengthened by ἅμ’ ἄμφω ‘both together’. The cowherd is not named here; the swineherd is named Eumaeus at 203. συφορβός is ‘swineherd’, from σῦς ‘pig’ and φέρβω ‘feed’, and Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο is a genitive in -οιο, ‘of divine Odysseus’.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ αὐτὸς μετὰ τοὺς δόμου ἤλυθε δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l: and out himself after them from the house went heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus himself went out of the house after them.
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἤλυθε is tmesis for ἐξῆλθε; ἤλυθε is ἦλθε. αὐτός ‘himself’ marks him off from the two herdsmen who went first. μετὰ τούς is ‘after them’: μετά with the accusative means ‘in pursuit of’ here, and δόμου is the genitive ‘out of the house’. δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is ‘heavenly Odysseus’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἐκτὸς θυρέων ἔσαν ἠδὲ καὶ αὐλῆς,
φθεγξάμενός σφε ἔπεσσι προσηύδα μειλιχίοισι·
sentences.l:
But when indeed they were outside the doors and the courtyard too,
calling out, them with words he spoke to, gentle ones:
sentences.i: But when they were outside the doors and the courtyard as well, he called out and spoke to them with gentle words:
sentences.n: ἔσαν is ἦσαν, and ἐκτός takes the genitives θυρέων (uncontracted, Attic θυρῶν) and αὐλῆς ‘courtyard’. φθεγξάμενος is the aorist middle participle of φθέγγομαι ‘speak out, call’. σφε is the enclitic accusative ‘them’. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’; ἔπεσσι μειλιχίοισι is a dative plural ‘with gentle words’ (-εσσι and -οισι).

sentences.t:
βουκόλε καὶ σύ, συφορβέ, ἔπος τί κε μυθησαίμην,
ἦ αὐτὸς κεύθω;
sentences.l:
“Cowherd, and you, swineherd, a word should I speak,
or keep it hidden myself?
sentences.i: “Cowherd, and you, swineherd, shall I speak a word, or keep it to myself?
sentences.n: βουκόλε and συφορβέ are vocatives. ἔπος τί κε μυθησαίμην is ‘should I speak some word?’, an optative with κε in a question of deliberation. ἦ at the start of the second part is ‘or’. αὐτός is ‘by myself’ and κεύθω a subjunctive, ‘keep hidden’. The Greek question mark ends the unit.

sentences.t: φάσθαι δέ με θυμὸς ἀνώγει.
sentences.l: and to speak me my heart bids.
sentences.i: My heart bids me speak.
sentences.n: φάσθαι is the middle infinitive of φημί, ‘to speak’, and με is the accusative of the person bidden. θυμός is ‘heart’. ἀνώγει is a perfect with present sense, ‘bids’.

sentences.t:
ποῖοί κ’ εἶτ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ ἀμυνέμεν, εἴ ποθεν ἔλθοι
ὧδε μάλ’ ἐξαπίνης καί τις θεὸς αὐτὸν ἐνείκαι;
sentences.l:
What sort would you be to defend Odysseus, if from anywhere he came
so very suddenly, and some god also brought him?
sentences.i: What sort of men would you be, to defend Odysseus, if he were to come from somewhere, as suddenly as that, and some god were to bring him?
sentences.n: ποῖοι … εἶτε is ‘what sort would you be’: εἶτε (written κ’ εἶτ’) is the second plural optative of εἰμί, with κε. ἀμυνέμεν is the epic infinitive ‘to defend’, with the dative Ὀδυσῆϊ. εἴ ποθεν ἔλθοι is ‘if from somewhere he should come’. ὧδε μάλ’ ἐξαπίνης is ‘so very suddenly’. ἐνείκαι is the aorist optative of φέρω, ‘should bring’ (Attic ἐνέγκαι). τις θεός is ‘some god’.

sentences.t: ἤ κε μνηστήρεσσιν ἀμύνοιτ’ ἦ Ὀδυσῆϊ;
sentences.l: Either the suitors would you defend, or Odysseus?
sentences.i: Would you defend the suitors, or Odysseus?
sentences.n: ἤ … ἦ is ‘either … or’. ἀμύνοιτ’ is ἀμύνοιτε, a second plural optative with κε, ‘would you defend’; it is the verb of 195, and again takes the dative of the one defended.

sentences.t: εἴπαθ’ ὅπως ὑμέας κραδίη θυμός τε κελεύει.
sentences.l: Tell me how your heart and spirit order you.”
sentences.i: Tell me what your heart and spirit urge you to do.”
sentences.n: εἴπαθ’ is εἴπατε, the aorist imperative ‘tell’. ὑμέας is the uncontracted accusative ‘you’ (Attic ὑμᾶς). κραδίη θυμός τε is ‘heart and spirit’, two nouns with the one singular verb κελεύει ‘orders’. The English of the second layer says ‘urge’. This ends Odysseus’s question.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε βοῶν ἐπιβουκόλος ἀνήρ·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the man, the herdsman of the cattle:
sentences.i: Then the herdsman of the cattle spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν is the pronoun ‘him’, and αὖτε ‘in turn’. προσέειπε is ‘addressed’. The speaker is named only by his work: ἐπιβουκόλος is ‘herdsman’ (ἐπί, ‘in charge of’), and βοῶν ‘of the cattle’, with ἀνήρ ‘man’ filling out the line. The whole line is a reply-formula already shipped.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ, αἲ γὰρ τοῦτο τελευτήσειας ἐέλδωρ,
ὡς ἔλθοι μὲν κεῖνος ἀνήρ, ἀγάγοι δέ ἑ δαίμων·
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, would that this you would fulfil, the wish,
that may come that man, and may lead him a power;
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, if only you would fulfil this wish: that that man may come, and that some power may lead him;
sentences.n: Ζεῦ πάτερ is the vocative, ‘father Zeus’. αἲ γάρ with an optative expresses a wish, ‘if only’: τελευτήσειας is the aorist optative ‘you would fulfil’, and ἐέλδωρ ‘wish’ stands in apposition to τοῦτο. ὡς with the optatives ἔλθοι and ἀγάγοι continues the wish, ‘that he may come … and lead him’. κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος ‘that’; the man is not named. ἑ is the enclitic ‘him’. δαίμων is ‘some power’, an unnamed divine force. The second line repeats one already shipped.

sentences.t: γνοίης χ’ οἵη ἐμὴ δύναμις καὶ χεῖρες ἕπονται.
sentences.l: you would know what sort my power is, and how my hands follow.”
sentences.i: you would know what strength is mine, and how my hands go with it.”
sentences.n: γνοίης χ’ is the aorist optative of γιγνώσκω with κε, ‘you would know’. The ‘you’ is no longer Zeus: the speaker turns to the man who has asked. οἵη ἐμὴ δύναμις is ‘what sort my power is’, and ἕπονται is a plural verb with the two subjects δύναμις and χεῖρες, ‘follow’: his hands go where his strength leads. This ends the cowherd’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς δ’ αὔτως Εὔμαιος ἐπεύχετο πᾶσι θεοῖσι
νοστῆσαι Ὀδυσῆα πολύφρονα ὅνδε δόμονδε.
sentences.l:
And so in the same way Eumaeus prayed to all the gods
that Odysseus the much-minded return home to his own house.
sentences.i: In the same way Eumaeus prayed to all the gods that Odysseus of the many counsels should return to his own home.
sentences.n: ὣς δ’ αὔτως is ‘and in just the same way’, so Eumaeus joins the cowherd. Εὔμαιος is the swineherd, now named. ἐπεύχετο is ‘prayed’, with the dative πᾶσι θεοῖσι. νοστῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of νοστέω ‘return home’, giving what he prayed for. πολύφρονα is ‘much-minded’, the epithet translated every time. ὅνδε δόμονδε is the accusative of ὅδε ‘this’ with δόμον and the suffix -δε ‘to’, literally ‘to this house’, the house where they stand; the second line repeats one already shipped, and keeps its wording.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ τῶν γε νόον νημερτέ’ ἀνέγνω,
ἐξαῦτίς σφε ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.l:
But when indeed of them the mind unerring he recognised,
again them with words, answering, he addressed:
sentences.i: But when he had recognised their unerring minds, he answered them again, and spoke:
sentences.n: τῶν γε is the genitive of the pronoun, ‘of them’, and νόον νημερτέ’ is ‘mind, unerring’ (νημερτέα elided). νημερτής is ‘not missing the mark, unerring’, here ‘true’. ἀνέγνω is the aorist of ἀναγιγνώσκω, ‘recognised, knew for certain’. ἐξαῦτις is ‘again’, and σφε ‘them’. ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν is the two-verb formula ‘answering with words, he addressed’. The speech this line introduces opens the next part.
